To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

consumers' valuation (perceived attractiveness) of an advertised sale depends on the subjective probability that the consumer will find a desirable product at the advertised price and on the size of the subjective discount, and that these two variables are influenced by the advertised level of the discount, the fraction of items in the advertised stock that are on sale, and the store price image.

the effectiveness of tensile versus precise price claims is determined by the store price image, the fraction of stock that is on sale (or that can be inferred to be on sale), and the advertised level of the price discount.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effects of tensile versus precise price claims and the role of price image in consumers' valuation of advertised sales offers.
the role of tensile claims and how they affect consumers' responses to advertised price reductions.
the effects of price claim type on consumers' valuation of advertised sale offers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

tensile versus precise price claims have different effects on the valuation of advertised sale offers depending on the store's price image, the fraction of stock advertised to be on sale, and the advertised discount level.
tensile claims are effective when consumers have low expectations of finding desirable items on sale and when the advertised discount is high.
the effects of tensile versus precise price claims are determined by the fraction of items that are on sale, the price image of the store, and the distribution of quality among sale items.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we develop and test a conceptual framework to examine how consumer responses to price claims depend on key variables under the control of the advertising retailer.

tensile price claims can be more effective than precise claims in attracting consumers to stores when the advertised stock is small and when the advertised discount is large, but not when the advertised stock of items on sale and the advertised discount is small.
tensile claims may not be better or worse than precise claims in general, but that their effectiveness may depend on the context of the advertised sale offer.
The main takeaway from our work is that

tensile claims can be more effective than precise claims in attracting consumers to advertised deals, but only when the fraction of items in the advertised stock that are on sale is low and the discount is high.

retailers can design tensile versus precise price claims to be more effective depending on the price image of the store, the level of discount advertised, and the fraction or distribution of stock that is on sale.
tensile claims are not necessarily better than precise claims.
